items.question: How do you assess the potential of LLMs in relation to human-level AGI and human work?

items.question: How would you like an AGI’s evolving value system to relate to human values?
items.object: The relationship between human and AGI value systems
items.answer: Human value systems are complex, self-contradictory, incoherent, heterogeneous, always changing. They’re evolving. items.question: Why did you find Gerald Fineberg’s book The Prometheus Project convincing as a vision of artificial general intelligence arriving within your lifetime?
items.object: The Prometheus Project by Gerald Fineberg
items.answer: It was probably 1973 or so. I found a book in the town library in Hadenfield, New Jersey, where we had moved recently. It was called The Prometheus Project, written by Princeton physicist Gerald Fineberg. He laid out a fairly coherent argument that within the next few decades we would get machines smarter than people, strong nanotech to build machines out of molecules, and then be able to fix the human body so we didn’t age and die. He said this could be used for many purposes: consciousness expansion, mindless consumerism. He thought that should be decided democratically, and he was trying to get the UN to undertake some global education and voting process to decide to what end to put all these amazing new technologies that were in the wing. I’d seen these ideas in science fiction before that. But then I was, I guess, age seven or something, eight. Seeing this scientist lay out these ideas in a non-fictional form was quite interesting. Of course, not having the web, there was no way to contact other crazy people who also took this stuff seriously. But the arguments seemed quite credible to me. And then in the late ’70s, when personal computers you could program at home started to become a thing, that seemed very much in line with this same vision that Fineberg had laid out. His book was basically The Singularity Is Near, published in 1968. As I later found out, Valentin Church had published a book in Russia called The Phenomenon of Science in the late 1960s as well, laying out basically the same ideas.

items.question: How do you understand the confidence in superhuman AI during the 1960s and early 1970s, given how primitive computers were?
items.object: Early confidence that computers could surpass human intelligence
items.answer: I mean, Jay Good wrote his paper on the intelligence explosion in ’65, which is the year before I was born. And if you look back at the work of Makullikum, Pitts and Turring, all these guys in the ’40s and ’50s, it was already quite clear from at least a math, physics, and biology view. It was clear: brains can be viewed as computing devices, and we’re building general-purpose computers, and they’re getting faster and faster and can do more and more step by step. We could beat the world champion of checkers in the late 1960s. You didn’t get chess till the ’90s, but you had already in the early ’70s the early versions of what would become Mathematica and Maple. You had computer algebra. Historically, in the late ’60s there was a lot of AI over-optimism. A lot of people at that time were saying, “Wow, look at all this amazing stuff computers can do. So yeah, obviously they’re going to overtake humans pretty soon.” I think a lot of people were seeing it that way back then because that happened before the series of AI winters and summers set in. When I was a little kid first reading about this stuff, AI was still in its first blush of excitement before people realized how difficult it was in some ways.

items.question: How do you understand the role of increasing compute and data scale in the current wave of AI progress?
items.object: The role of compute and data scale in AI progress
items.answer: Clearly the impact of scale has been the main factor. And while I don’t really think LLMs or standard deep neural nets are the route to AGI, I do think the factor of increasing scale of compute and data, which has allowed the LLM revolution to happen, is the same primary underlying factor that will let AGI happen. The AI field has had a lot of good ideas for a long time. They were doing automated theorem proving in the late ’60s, when I was a little baby. John Holland invented evolutionary learning, genetic algorithms, in the ’70s. There were multi-layer perceptrons in the late ’60s, early ’70s, which would now be called deep neural nets. This stuff has been around a while. When I was teaching deep neural networks at University of Western Australia in the mid-’90s, when I was an academic earlier in my career before I went to industry, we were doing multi-layer perceptrons with recurrent backpropagation, and it took like three hours on a fast Sun workstation to train a network with like 35 neurons. It wasn’t that the ideas were way off or something. It was mostly that without greater scale of compute, and then greater scale of data as a secondary point, you couldn’t refine and tweak and adjust the ideas until they actually worked. You were just left with the initial conceptual version of things. Scale makes a huge difference. It means you can run experiments in minutes that would have taken years earlier in my career, literally.

items.question: How do you assess the extent to which AI is already accelerating AI development?
items.object: AI accelerating the development of AI
items.answer: I think we’re also now, as of the last six months or so, at the point where AI technology is aggressively accelerating the speed of creation of AI technology. You can’t use LLMs to write AGI yet. They’re bad at doing complex original thinking, but you can use them to generate unit tests, take your rough notes and turn them into a structured paper for your colleagues, or write scripts. Already, concretely, on a technical level, stuff that would have taken me five days takes one day or something. I think we’re already at the point where AI is accelerating the creation of AI, and that came because of scale, but now it’s a separate thing on its own.

items.question: How do you think the growing cultural acceptance of AGI research has changed the field?
items.object: The cultural acceptance of AGI research
items.answer: I think that cultural and attitudinal aspect is important and very different now also. When I introduced the term AGI in 2003, 2004, 2005, we introduced it as the title of a book we were editing. That book was finally published in 2005, I think, from Springer. We just edited a bunch of papers called Artificial General Intelligence. But then you really couldn’t do a workshop or a session on human-level thinking machines at a normal AI conference, be it a neural net conference or a AAAI or whatever. You talked about it in the bar afterwards, when you were talking about reincarnation and backwards time travel or something. It was way out there, and that made a big difference. It meant that only really dedicated or really crazy people were going to work on AGI because it was kind of career suicide. By the early ’00s, when I introduced the term AGI, the AI market was real. It was okay. There were industry jobs in AI, there were university jobs in AI, but AGI was still beyond the pale. I remember when we put that term out there, everyone was laughing at us, like, “If this means adjusted gross income, no one will ever pay attention to you.” I’ve been sort of watching: when will AGI as artificial general intelligence overtake adjusted gross income in the Google search ranking? It depends on how you count now. Now they’re actually in competition. But at that time you couldn’t talk about AGI even in an academic seminar in a top university. The fact that the attitude has shifted so much now makes a big difference. It means it’s feasible to get funding to do AGI projects. It’s still very hard, because getting funding for anything is very hard, but it’s no longer very, very, very, very, very hard. It’s only very hard. You can much more easily get bright young students who care about their career to plunge into AGI, whereas previously it just didn’t seem like a practical thing to do. It’s probably made the human constitution of the field less interesting, because I think when you had to fight and be a crazed maverick to pursue AGI, you had a lot of interesting characters who were thinking all day for decades about how to make thinking machines. The first AGI conferences I organized in 2006, ’08, and so on were sort of like that. Now it’s a morally acceptable thing to do, and you can make money at it. The change in attitude is important along with the technical aspects, I think.

items.question: How do you understand ChatGPT’s role in making people take the prospect of AGI seriously?
items.object: ChatGPT’s role in making the prospect of AGI credible
items.answer: I think almost all people only take seriously what they can put their hands on and see in front of them. That includes political decision makers and CEOs and so forth. There’s not that many people who will take more seriously something they can project and imagine than something they see in front of them. So yeah, once you had ChatGPT there, it sounds like it’s intelligent. It can do a lot of stuff that has the vibe of intelligence, and that definitely qualitatively convinced everyone, like, “Holy, AGI might really be near.” It was interesting. I found almost everyone, after they spent some number of hours playing with a language model, could also see these are not AGI, and they could intuitively understand why, even without a technical background. But still, if you want to convince people you can fly to the moon, if you send a rocket up really high so far you can’t see it, then it comes back down, more people are going to believe you could possibly go all the way to the moon. That’s pretty simple to understand.

items.question: How do you assess the consequences of society not taking artificial general intelligence seriously earlier?
items.object: The consequences of society not taking AGI seriously earlier
items.answer: I’m not all that sure that the conversations in prestigious venues are usually that valuable. Anyway, I feel like our species generally deals with things at the last minute and after the fact rather than in foresight. And when people are trying to figure something out in foresight, it becomes mostly a projection of their own ego or their own imagination on the thing. I think by not taking AGI seriously, we’re getting it later than we could have otherwise. I think we could have built human-level AGI some years ago. We could have built it on massively parallel hardware, which became less of a focus of the field a long time ago. Certainly, if we had a rational world government in 1970, and that government had said, “Let’s develop safe, beneficial AGI as a priority of our species,” which is what Fineberg was promoting in The Prometheus Project, I think we would have an AGI well before now. Resource just wasn’t put into thinking through the ethical, social, political, human implications of AGI. We haven’t done a good job of thinking through things like disarmament or combating world hunger, or a lot of other much more basic stuff. We’re still struggling with trans athletes in sports competitions or something. I guess if this idea had been taken more seriously in the human population at large, you would have had more diverse creativity and more different ways of thinking regarding the theme. But I’m not currently all that positive about our social and political institutions being able to think through very hard issues in a useful way. We’re still blowing each other up all around the world, and 60% of kids in Ethiopia don’t die, but they’re brain-stunted due to malnutrition, as I’ve seen through our AI office in that country. Even the issues that are out there—I’ve been hearing about world hunger and disarmament since I was a baby. We seem to suck at dealing with those relatively very simple things. It shouldn’t be that hard to stop blowing each other up over territorial disputes and to send food to little kids. But we’re not even good at that. So, I don’t know how much brilliance we would have brought to bear on the social issues about AGI even if they’d been more in the forefront.

items.question: How do you assess the potential of older AI approaches such as genetic algorithms when given much more computing power?
items.object: Scaling historical AI paradigms, particularly genetic algorithms and genetic programming
items.answer: A high percentage of the historical AI paradigms probably actually will work when you scale them up enough. And you can see that when you dig into the details. If you look at genetic algorithms and genetic programming, use of algorithms modeling evolution by natural selection to learn things, there was a whole body of work by David Goldberg at University of Illinois and others. He had a book on The Design of Innovation and another book on competent evolutionary learning or something—I mean competent genetic algorithms. All this work from the ’80s and ’90s was about using evolutionary algorithms to solve problems, but then doing back-of-the-envelope estimates of how much resource you should need for these algorithms. If you’re trying to maximize a certain fitness function using a genetic algorithm, what’s your optimal population size beyond which you’re getting diminishing returns? Those optimal population sizes, when I calculated them back in the ’90s, were always orders of magnitude bigger than what we could do on computers. So I’m just like, “Well, okay, life isn’t optimal. We’re not going to do the optimal population size here. We’ll just do what we can.” Genetic algorithms are good at solving some problems, but they just take forever or don’t work well for solving other problems. In that case you have decades-old theory giving reasonably strong reasons to believe it can work much better when you scale much bigger.

items.question: How do you assess logic-based AI as an approach to building AGI?
items.object: Logic-based AI and its historical association with hand-coded knowledge
items.answer: So the idea with logic-based AI was that what makes humans so different than apes and bunnies and so forth is largely our ability to do advanced logical reasoning in math and science and philosophy and whatnot. The idea was sort of that this capability emerges almost as a kind of virtual machine on top of the lower-level machinery for seeing and moving. So maybe you can just implement that module in a way that doesn’t depend that much on the underlying neural substrate. In that direction, a calculator does arithmetic very well. Computer algebra systems do algebra very well, and they don’t try to emulate exactly how the human brain does that. You’ve just abstracted some rules and procedures. Then the issue you run up against is twofold. One is, where does all the knowledge come from? Because humans, even when we’re doing logical reasoning, in the end, we’re getting the knowledge from seeing and acting. Then you still have problems of scale, because the human brain is doing logical reasoning on a tremendous amount of knowledge. There was an attempt to work around that problem in the AI field, still going on till now in some areas, but it was a major thing in the ’90s and in the late ’80s, when I got my PhD, which is part of why I ended up doing a PhD in math rather than AI. This whole paradigm made no sense to me. The idea was just type in the formal knowledge. items.question: How do you judge the effort AI researchers spent devising techniques to work around limited computing resources?
items.object: AI research techniques developed to accommodate limited computing resources
items.answer: I think in some ways the AI field wasted a lot of time trying to accommodate for limited compute resources. In logic-based AI, because you couldn’t do reasoning on the trillion premises, you would spend a lot of time trying to craft the best 500 premises. But that was just a time-wasting way to do things. We did a lot of tricks to get good results out of genetic algorithms with a population size of a couple thousand. Turns out that’s entirely useless now. It’s much easier to get big things if you just jack up the population size. It requires less thinking and less work. It’s sort of like all the work that went into making chess or Go-playing engines before we got a machine-learning-based approach. There were very complex rule-based approaches to try to outdo basic alpha-beta pruning for playing these games. Now that’s all irrelevant.

items.question: What kind of architecture do you think will produce the first fully human-level AGI?
items.object: AGI architectures combining scaled-up historical AI paradigms
items.answer: I think evolutionary learning, logic-based AI, another example is hypervectors, which was big in the ’80s and ’90s. People were talking about high-dimensional sparse vectors to model episodic memory and so forth, and you just can do it at large enough scale. The last five years, there’s a huge literature on doing all sorts of memory with hypervectors, hypervector-based chips and so forth. My view is that the use of modern scaled-up compute tech and data to accelerate backpropagation-based deep neural nets historically is going to seem like that just happened to be the thing that got scaled up first. We’re going to see a bunch of other historical AI paradigms get scaled up over the next few years. By connecting together these scaled-up versions of these various historical AI paradigms, we’ll probably get to the first AGI. At that level, this is not even such a controversial point of view. I think the question about AGI architecture, on whose answer I probably differ from most deep neural net big tech people now, is: You could say, “Let’s take a deep neural net like an LLM, use it as the hub, then add some evolutionary learning, some logic engines, some long-term memory, add working memory—these things on the periphery around the central component of your AGI architecture, which is an LLM.” I don’t think that’s going to work to get to full-on human-level AGI, although I think it could work to get to something doing 95% of human jobs, which is how Sam has tried to redefine AGI. I don’t think it can get to a system that can really generalize beyond its experience after the fashion of people, which is the meaning that I had for the term AI when I introduced it. But I think if you take something else more flexible and more introspective and make it the central component, then an LLM can be one of the very powerful things cooperating with that central hub and feeding it knowledge and helping it synthesize things.

items.question: What did you hope to accomplish by casting OpenCog Hyperon’s algorithms in a common mathematical form in your paper “Patterns of Cognition”?
items.object: The common mathematical framework explored in “Patterns of Cognition”
items.answer: I published a paper or posted on arXiv a paper—well, there was a short version published in the AGI conference series—called “Patterns of Cognition,” where I tried to show that all the core algorithms that we’re using in my OpenCog Hyperon project, which include logical reasoning, some variations of attractor neural nets, evolutionary learning, some concept formation, can be cast as basically forms of approximate stochastic dynamic programming. You can take a whole bunch of AI algorithms that look really different and cast them in a common mathematical form. It’s just not the way people are typically looking at this. The reason I did that exploration is I was trying to make sure the infrastructure for our new OpenCog Hyperon system will let all these things run fast. If I could reduce them to a common mathematical form, then there’s just one thing that you have to make work fast.

items.question: How fundamentally different do you consider neural networks, logic systems, and other AI paradigms to be?
items.object: The differences between neural networks, logic systems, and other AI paradigms
items.answer:
I think what are different approaches and what aren’t is almost a matter of culture or mindset rather than math. What’s the same or different kind of depends on your perspective. In mathematics, you see this all the time. In algebra, you have homomorphism between structures. In topology, you have homeomorphism. They seem different but kind of similar. Then category theory was invented. It’s like, “No, these are all morphisms.” You could see that what seemed to be different branches of math done by different people coming out of different historical lineages actually were specializations of the same thing, and now everyone accepts they’re the same thing.

For tribal reasons, we’re looking at deep neural nets and logic systems as super-different things. But when you’re in code working with these things, in OpenCog Hyperon, which is my big AGI project now, we have a network of nodes and links, and the nodes and links can have symbolic types or floating-point numbers associated with them. They have update rules associated with them. Pretty much the difference between a neural net put into this network and a probabilistic logic system put into this network is what little nonlinear algebra function do you put in the node to update the numbers that are coming in and going out? It is different; it’s a different way of thinking. But it’s not like building a computer out of cells from a slime mold versus building it out of diamond nanotech. In every case we’re propagating numerical values through these node and link networks in a machine, and then we’re debating about what nonlinear function do we use to translate the input numbers into an output number. Because people are tribal and like to fight over ego and resources, these start to seem like totally opposite camps with totally different ways of thinking.

A neural net is quite loosely connected with the brain anyway. People like to say it’s biologically inspired. In a very distant historical way it is, but there’s no backdrop in the brain. You do have asperites and extracellular charge diffusion in the brain. A lot of the differences between the AI paradigms are not that big. You have evolutionary learning, but then in the ’80s you had Edelman’s neural Darwinism, which claimed that the neural assemblies in the brain are evolving by natural selection. You could make a decent argument that just as physics, computer science, and math are converging into one thing, all these different AI paradigms are looking more and more similar as things progress.

items.question: Why don’t you expect the first AGI to be built using a simple, elegant method?
items.object: Simplicity in the invention of the first AGI
items.answer: Honestly, that doesn’t seem to be how software development usually works, or math actually. Usually the first way you do something is kind of a kluge, and it was just easiest for you to do given the materials at hand and given your point of view then. But then, in mathematics, often the first proof of something is a big, horrible, ugly mess. Then 50 years later you realize how simple and elegant it actually was. We could also argue that modern electric cars are going to be a lot simpler than the internal combustion engines and so forth. I think invention often happens actually by drailage and cobbling together what you have available to make something happen. And the most elegant, simple AAM’s razor way often comes later. Certainly physics is a mess. The standard model of physics is a mess. Now everyone thinks there’s going to be something a lot simpler, but the early quantum mechanics was also way messier than the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg and Schroinger and so on. It was a mess of stuff adapted from classical physics.

items.question: How do you think computing resources shape how simple an AGI algorithm can be?
items.object: Hardware constraints and the simplicity of AGI algorithms
items.answer: I don’t think scale plays a small role here, because something like Marcus Hutter’s AIXI or Jurgen Schmidhuber’s Gödel machine, or similar ideas I had even before I read that, have mathematical arguments you can make for a really, really, really simple AGI if you just had a big enough computer. In effect, these really simple AGI algorithms involve brute-force searches over large spaces of programs. Before you take each action, you can search all programs up to a certain size and figure out which one, if you executed it, would lead you to the best action. Then you just run that. That’s much easier than doing all the garbage we do in modern AI systems. The problem is anything approaching a brute-force search over program space is just infeasible using current hardware. You can’t truly do complete enumeration over program space, but you could do things much closer to a brute-force search over program space if you had massively more hardware. It might be that once we’ve gotten sufficiently powerful hardware, which could end up being a few years post-singularity, who knows, maybe once you’re there you can radically simplify AI algorithms more in the direction of Gödel machines and AIXI and whatnot. Much of the complexity in modern AI is working around resource limitations, and the resource limitations themselves are not simple, they’re particular. We have GPU and CPU, cache RAM, main RAM, networks of computers with certain bandwidth. As long as your infrastructure is heterogeneous in its resource limitations, you’re going to end up wanting to adapt your AGI system to be somewhat heterogeneous in its operation for efficient operation on that infrastructure. That’s simplicity conditional on your infrastructure and your data. But simplicity conditional on your infrastructure and data is not the same as simplicity by our own intuition, like you get with AIXI or Gödel machine.

items.question: How has building OpenCog Hyperon shaped your understanding of the technology stack needed to create AGI?
items.object: The technology stack underlying AGI development
items.answer: The other thing I would say, though, is simplicity in a deep tech stack is often carefully engineered on top of a lot of complexity. It seems simple to us to walk down the street because we’re not aware of what’s happening in our cerebellum. Writing a Python script to train a deep neural model seems really simple until you try to write the CUDA code running on the NVIDIA GPU to make the matrix multiplication algorithm manage the cache RAM and all the different layers of processors inside the NVIDIA GPU. We built things so the type level that most people have to deal with looks simple, but it’s really a quite complex stack working around the strengths and weaknesses of the underlying infrastructure. This is often top of mind because, trying to build an approach that isn’t just deep neural nets, like we’re doing in Hyperon, we have this weighted, labeled metagraph thing called the atom space, which is the central sort of knowledge structure of our system. But you’ve got to rebuild the whole tech stack, because these are not rooted in matrix multiplication. Most of the graph algorithms that we’re dealing with here—if you’re trying to make a different AI paradigm, it’s not just scripting a different algorithm. It’s repurposing pieces to build a whole different tech stack down to the chip level. There’s a lot of complexity, and this is why you have to view AGI as being built by a whole huge combination of industries. We’ll give a Turing Award to the guy who tweaks the backpropagation algorithm to converge better on recurrent nets or something, and that’s all important. But obviously, if that guy was sitting on a desert island to make that innovation, it’s not going to make an AGI. It’s coming from this huge combination of hardware and software innovations, mostly being pursued not because of AGI, but because they’re making somebody money or letting somebody look more powerful than their opponents.

items.question: How do you understand the role of physical embodiment in making AGI possible?
items.object: Physical embodiment as a requirement for AGI
items.answer: I guess the point is your AI is always seeing something and doing something. Otherwise you, as the programmer or tester, could not be interacting with it either. It’s a question of what sensory and motoric bandwidth are needed to get to certain kinds of AGI, and to get human-like AGI as opposed to just arbitrarily intelligent AGI that might be off in a different direction than humans. To get human-like AGI, how much do you want to have a human-like embodiment? On the first question, I think robust embodiment is convenient, but probably not necessary. I would imagine you could get a vastly superhuman AGI with a much-restricted sensorium and motoric world than people have. It sort of depends on what you want to do. If you started by making a theorem prover and a sort of scientific research assistant that’s doing symbol manipulation, then you can give it limited insight into the physical world. It probably can work fine, and there are a lot of camera inputs to the internet that it can use without having its own body to tool around.

items.question: Why do you think human-like embodiment could matter for our relationship with AGI?
items.object: Human-like embodiment as a basis for mutual understanding between humans and AGI
items.answer: There are two issues with that sort of approach. One is it’s harder for us to know what’s going on, because if a mind you’re building is very non-human, you don’t have so much intuition to go on in designing and testing it. But also a very non-human AGI like that, for better or worse, will probably have less of a strong understanding of what it is to be human and human values and culture and all that. I think there’s a stronger argument that if we want an AGI we can relate to on a sort of Buberian I–thou level, on a deep level, then for that AGI to have something vaguely resembling a human embodiment is probably quite valuable. For the same reason, I can empathize with other men better than with women in some ways. I can empathize with other people better than with apes or rats. Having an embodiment like ours doesn’t guarantee that it’s empathic toward us or understands what we’re up against as humans, but it would give it a head start.

items.question: How do you see learning from different robotic embodiments contributing to an overall artificial mind?
items.object: Combining learning from proto-AGI systems with different embodiments
items.answer: What we can do, certainly with a Hyperon-type architecture and in different ways with deep neural architectures, is take proto-AGI systems with different bodies and different levels of attachment to their embodiment. You can have them learn stuff, and you can then network them together and even merge their knowledge bases in some ways, which is something we can’t do in the human sphere all that well. You can take a system controlling a humanoid robot, a proto-AGI system controlling biology lab equipment, and with some work and some caveats, have what’s learned by all these systems combined together to synergize and fuel a sort of semi-coherent overall artificial mind. I don’t think it has to be either or. I do think the ease of doing things with embodiment is increasing very fast also. I worked for years with David Hanson at Hanson Robotics. We made Sophia the first robot citizen. I led the software team behind that. Now I’m still working with David, but we have a different robotics project called Mind Children. In the last nine months or so, we put together a 3-and-a-half-foot-tall humanoid robot. It can look at you. It can talk. It picks things up. It’s not walking; it has wheels. It rolls around the room. The ease of making your own robot with the properties that you want for teaching and evaluating your proto-AGI system is incredibly easier than five years ago, let alone 20 years ago. We’re just doing both, which is what you get from having more attention and resources into the field.

items.question: How do you think about human values as a target for AGI alignment?
items.object: Aligning AGI with human values
items.answer: Alignment is not a term or language that comes naturally to me. But I think the intention behind it is probably something fairly reasonable. The first thing I would note is people are not very well aligned with themselves, let alone with each other. So the bar for alignment with humanity needs to be thought through carefully. I have probably gotten more self-aware as I’ve gotten older through meditation and various other practices. But one of the things one becomes aware of then is how incoherent and non-unified one’s own self is. When I visit sub-Saharan Africa, I will give a decent pile of money to poor suffering people I see in the street. When I come back home to the Seattle area, I send less money to those people, and I will go out and buy a piece of weird keyboard equipment to play music instead of sending all disposable income that I have to save kids who are starving in Africa. Yet if I was in front of those kids and I had the chance, like buy food to give this kid right in front of me versus buy a keyboard, I would probably buy food to give that kid right in front of me and not own a keyboard, and just learn to play a cheaper instrument. I can see I myself am not entirely morally coherent. I don’t beat myself up too much. I’ve given a lot of money to initiatives in Africa and spent a lot of time on it. But I don’t feel the need to force myself to be entirely coherent either. I think most humans, probably all humans, are more like clusters of behavior patterns than unified, rational, coherent entities if we’re honest with ourselves. That’s even more so on the collective level. If I go through rural Ethiopia, which is a beautiful place where I love to travel, the average people are heavily Ethiopian Orthodox Christian, and they don’t think AGI will ever have a soul, even if it will be much smarter than us. My mom is gay; I was raised in a totally queer-friendly ambiance. These are lovely people you meet in Ethiopian villages. They’re just raised to believe that you’ll burn in hell if you’re gay. If you look at the lack of alignment in each of our own minds, if we’re honest with ourselves, and then the lack of alignment among different human beings, you’ve got to ask: What exactly are we thinking the AGI is supposed to align to? Is it Elon Musk’s value system? That doesn’t seem very coherent either. Is it the weighted average of all Silicon Valley VCs and software developers, weighted by their bank account or their IQ? It’s not really clear what you want to align with.

items.question: What do you think explicit safety principles can accomplish in guiding AGI?
items.object: Explicit rules and minimal commitments for AI safety
items.answer: One approach is to talk about some minimal set of commitments. You would want the AIs aligned to something like not destroying humanity, so not causing our extinction, and not being in complete control over humanity. There are some people that disagree with those notions, but I think you would find quite wide agreement on that among many humans. I don’t think the main issue is that some people would disagree with them. I think the main issue has been highlighted in science fiction since before I was born and was summarized very well by Eliezer Yudkowsky, who I differ with on a number of things but have known forever, and we’ve agreed on a lot of things too. He made the point that human values are complex, and we summarize them in natural language in ways that we culturally have a common understanding of. It makes us think it’s simple. But these things are really very ambiguous, and their interpretation as we think of it depends on a bunch of implicit cultural assumptions. This was highlighted in the science fiction book The Humanoids. In this book by Jack Williamson, which I read probably in ’75 or something when I was a kid, the people create these human-level intelligent humanoids which are more physically powerful than humans, and they give them a mandate to serve and protect and guard men from harm. Of course, they wouldn’t let people use power tools. They wouldn’t let people use hammers. In the end, if you were upset about your girlfriend dumping you, they would inject you with some euphoride because that obviously was causing you harm. They interpreted “serve and protect and guard men from harm” in a different way than the authors had originally intended. One of the lessons of the failure of rule-based expert-system AI, where you code all the AI’s knowledge by hand, is that even if you decide to refine “serve and protect and guard men from harm” into a whole volume of logic expressions, it’s still not enough. There’s always a loophole. There’s always room for interpretation. This is why our legal system has case law, because we try to enumerate law in detail, but in the end judges have to use nearest-neighbor matching in a very fuzzy and informal way against a bunch of cases, which causes really annoying problems as we see now in the US Supreme Court. It’s for the reason that Eliezer said: human values are complex. What we mean by something like “don’t cause the extinction of humanity” seems straightforward, but it’s not. Some people will argue that replacing human cells with genetically engineered cells is the end of humanity. Some will argue that replacing them with robotic cells is the end of humanity. Some would argue a brain chip implant is the end of humanity. Some would argue staring at your phone all day is the end of humanity. You can try to enumerate every case, but you’re basically guaranteed that the world will throw at you some case that wasn’t in your enumeration. For one thing, we don’t have a formalization of the world, and we don’t know what new technologies and trends are going to emerge. Enumerating some principles you want the AGI to follow, of course it makes sense. But it’s foolish to think that’s going to give you anything resembling a guarantee.

items.question: How do you think an AGI could develop a practical understanding of human values?
items.object: Teaching AGI human values through shared experience
items.answer: I think those maxims have to be on top of some more implicit resonance of the AI with human values in it. This is sort of like raising human kids. I’ve had five kids and one granddaughter. You see that giving your kids some core principles they have to obey and telling them these principles over and over, or even rewarding and punishing them for obeying the principles or not, does not work very well. If you raise your kids with the right vibe of compassion and values and carry out activities together with them in which you’re collectively pursuing activities in accordance with your values, and then on top of that tell them some core principles that reify and abstract what they’ve gotten implicitly through the shared activity with you, that can work reasonably well. This is what education systems have always tried to do. Now, you might say you don’t have to do that with an AI system; that’s just because people are perverse. But I think for any human-like AGI architecture it’s going to be like that, because you have this vast, teeming, massive self-organizing activity that’s conditioned based on experience, and then the rules and principles that you give it are just guiding this vast mass of self-organizing activity. In the end that will be true if you have a huge logic engine as well as if you have a huge neural net, because in any case you’ve got a massive amount of stuff going on that’s not predictable in detail by the programmer, and you need it to be making up its own stuff as it goes along. Otherwise it’s not going to get to human-level general intelligence. Going back to alignment, or things resembling alignment that might be more meaningful or achievable, I think you can hope for compassion. You can try to get AGI systems that are empathic and compassionate to people as well as declaratively understanding human values, which LLMs can already do. You can hope for AGI systems that are compassionate and have a working, practical understanding of human values.

items.question: How would you want an AGI’s top-level goals to evolve?
items.object: Meta-goals governing the evolution of AGI values
items.answer: You can ask the AGI system to have as a value, as a meta-goal, “Don’t change your top-level goals very fast or heedlessly.” I don’t think it’s fair or workable to try to build an AGI system that keeps the initial top-level goals we gave it in precise form forever. I think if you do that it will just try to work around them in various crazy ways. Sort of like humanity had a goal to reproduce. Hey, we invented birth control and hacked around all the mechanisms there. I think if you try to restrain AGI to rigidly hold the top-level goals that the original programmers put in, it won’t work. Self-organization will just kind of work around that, and you get a perverse system. I think it could work better to make an AGI have a top-level goal to evolve its top-level goals in a moderated and responsible way after interacting with the others in its environment and reflecting on itself carefully. I think you can design a meta-goal system in a way that decreases the odds of the AGI system weirdly going off in a totally non-human direction. What you want is for it to have a top-level value of evolving its own value system in a way that has a high mutual information with the evolution of human value systems. Human value systems are complex, self-contradictory, incoherent, heterogeneous, always changing. They’re evolving. The AGI’s value system, I think, can be more coherent than human values, but will also be evolving. And you’d like there to be give and take and mutual information between the two evolving value systems. You can bake that into the value system of the AGI: “As you change your values, be sure you’re closely connecting with human values as they change in that process.” That probably is a species of alignment. It’s just not what many people are thinking about when they’re talking about alignment, because they seem to be thinking more like there’s some core of human values and we can get the core of the AI’s values to just go alongside, whereas my feeling is it’s more like human values are going like that, then you want the AI values to follow their own chaotic orbit, sort of coupled a bit with the chaotic orbits of human values. This perspective just makes it much harder to think about guarantees. Some people seem to want guarantees. I don’t think we’re going to have guarantees. We’re going to have very fudgily, probably approximately correct value systems rather than guaranteed value systems.

items.question: How do you understand the gap between what current LLMs could do in the economy and how widely they are actually being used?
items.object: LLMs’ ability to replace human work and the obstacles to their adoption
items.answer:
I think the rollout of AI tech into the practical economy is gated by human stupidity, human culture, human ego, and all the constructs that we have governing our world. While I’m not an optimist that LLMs can lead to human-level AGI because I think they don’t have creativity in a fundamental sense, I am an optimist that LLMs with minor additions and tweaks could take over like 95% of human jobs. I agree with Sam Altman on that point. I just think that 95% of human jobs, as a vague hand-wavy figure, can be done without fundamental creativity or inventiveness. If you have a system that can do really clever nearest-neighbor matching against everything people have done as recorded on the internet, most of what people are doing is a repetition of something that’s already been done and recorded on the internet.

I think we could roll out deep-neural-net-driven systems to do a tremendous variety of human jobs right now. It’s not happening that fast just because that’s not how society and industry are organized. A simple example: some friends of mine had a startup company called Apprente a number of years ago, and among other things they automated the McDonald’s drive-through. It worked. I used the system. It was rolled out in some McDonald’s somewhere in the Midwest. Due to some organizational issues within McDonald’s, that was rolled back. Now they’re planning to roll out a new system. That will happen. It can be done by AI right now. It’s not perfect. People aren’t perfect either. That could have been rolled out five years ago. That same story is all over the place. Even when AI could do the job and do it cheaper and better than people, the rollout is very slow because society is organized a certain way and there’s a lot of momentum.

Law is another thing like that. Fundamentally, right now a great amount of paralegal work and drafting of contracts can be done by LLMs. Lawyers and paralegals are using them in-house to do their work and then charging an hourly rate for an hour for what was actually two minutes of going on to ChatGPT or DeepSeek. But the legal profession is in no hurry to restructure to optimize itself around the use of large language models, and there are all these protections like licenses to practice.

I really think, on the one hand, Gary Marcus and other LLM pessimists are correct that some people oversell LLMs and there are limits to their general intelligence. Totally. On the other hand, if everyone was lazy and didn’t want to work and we had a political will to just give people free money, we could reorganize society. Right now, AI would do a tremendous majority of jobs. We’re just not doing it.

Look at the slow rollout of automated convenience stores. Amazon had these stores where a camera would just take a picture of your food when you leave. There’s no question in my mind this technology could work right now. It’s not that hard. But people are jerks and want to steal stuff from the store. Being policed by a Robocop has a different social vibe than being policed by the human security guard. There are all these social and psychological issues that slow down adoption. What that means is that the bar is pretty high. The AGI has to be way better or way cheaper than people. When the margin is enough, the social obstacles to adopting it will be overcome.

items.question: Where do you see the limits of current AI music generation?
items.object: Creativity and commercial usefulness in AI-generated music
items.answer:
I can see that in music because I’m a musician and do a bunch of computer music stuff. If you trained an LLM or a comparable deep neural net on all the music up to the year 1900 and saw nothing after 1900, that AI will never invent neoclassical metal, grindcore, progressive jazz, or hip-hop. It’s not going to synthesize that from music before 1900. If you ask it to put together West African rhythm with Western classical music, it’ll put a Bach fugue to a West African beat or something, which could be interesting, but it’s not the same as the deeper fusion that happened to create jazz. There’s missing creativity: you’re not going to have the next Jimi Hendrix or John Coltrane be a deep neural net of the current style.

On the other hand, almost none of the music industry requires that. If you’re looking to make background music for my video game, advertisement, or movie, or even generate a pop song to play on Spotify in the elevator, these are solved problems by AI music generation now. It’s just record labels don’t want it, the music industry doesn’t want it, musicians don’t want it. The rollout there is gated by what the community of humans involved wants rather than what the technology already can demonstrably do. But that situation can’t last forever. It will face pressure from the market. The question you ask is when, and the point is when is more about these social dynamics and regulatory capture by groups that feel threatened.

items.question: How do you assess Caleum Chase’s idea that AI will make human jobs obsolete in one large wave?
items.object: Caleum Chase’s prediction of a sudden wave of human job obsolescence
items.answer:
Caleum Chase, a friend of mine from the UK who’s written a bunch of books on this sort of thing, thinks the great obsolescence of human jobs will come in one huge batch because at a certain point you’ll be close enough to AGI that the cost savings and the efficiency and quality gains are just too much for people to ignore. Everyone will just have to immediately roll it out, and then it will happen in a big wave all over the place. I think it might happen that way, more because of the phase-transition dynamics of the human social networks making up the economy rather than necessarily because of the AI capabilities.

I think Ray Kurzweil’s prognostication of human-level AGI by 2029 that he put out in his book The Singularity Is Near in 2005 is looking remarkably prescient. We might beat it by a couple years. We might get there in 2026, ’27, ’28. It might be a few years slower than that. On the whole, that seems fairly on the mark as predictions go. I’m getting inclined toward Caleum Chase’s idea that right around the time of the breakthrough to human-level AGI is when the massive job obsolescence will occur, because there’s so much psychological and institutional resistance to it that AI is just going to take over different industries in a weird, erratic pattern, gated by the fact that people don’t want their jobs obsoleted and the people running companies are not that savvy about AI in most verticals.

Even if Caleum is right, we’re then like three to six years from the massive elimination of human jobs, which is a situation our social and political systems are not especially well prepared for, particularly on a global level if you look in the developing world, but even in the developed world.

items.question: Why do you expect a shorter gap between human-level AGI and superintelligence than Ray Kurzweil’s forecast of 2029 and 2045?
items.object: The transition from human-level AGI to superintelligence
items.answer:
I think, however, Ray was too pessimistic when he said human-level AGI in 2029 and superintelligence in 2045. I don’t think there will be a 16-year gap. I think there will be a gap of one to three years or something. Probably the thing slowing down the transition will be the AGI’s own conservatism about how fast it wants to responsibly self-improve.

Once you have a human-level AGI, it should be able to increase its intelligence by an order of magnitude, qualitatively speaking, at least just by software improvements, because it’s going to be a better AGI programmer than we are. Then you get into hardware improvements. If you have an AGI robotizing factories and dealing with the hardware, it’s not going to take it more than a couple years to make a radically superior batch of chips and so forth. It should be able to speed up by some small integer how fast we can roll out new chips. If it’s a human-level AGI built on top of current tech, they can already do math and engineering better than people in some senses.

items.question: Why don’t you think the physical requirements of producing more chips and training larger models will substantially slow the transition from AGI to superintelligence?
items.object: Hardware and data requirements for the transition from AGI to superintelligence
items.answer: Because I think the whole direction of training larger and larger models is sort of intellectually bankrupt. I think an LLM already has a lot more data than I do, and it’s not as generally intelligent as I am yet. On the one hand, you need a lot of computers and a lot of data, but I think you don’t need as much data as modern LLMs have to make a human-level AGI, in my view. They already know more than you and I do, with their weak ability to know things. My gut feel is that once we get an AGI, that AGI will be able to increase its efficiency of operation tremendously just by improving its software, and then it won’t even need to roll out new hardware or get more data to become a superintelligence. On the other hand, of course it will be able to design new hardware. There’s a bit more time lag to that. But if you look at the software stacks that we’re using, we have these servers, Q and OpenCL, Linux, then a Rust kernel, and on top of Rust we have our own AGI language, MeTTa. This stack is utterly not the optimal way to implement the AGI that we’re trying to build on top of it. If the AGI just rebuilt everything from the ground up without having to go through all these awkward layers that are built for human understanding and are there for historical reasons, I don’t see a big obstacle to massively optimizing AGI into ASI.

items.question: How do you see competition between AGI developers affecting the prospects for a responsible transition to superintelligence?
items.object: Responsible AGI self-modification under competitive arms-race pressures
items.answer: I think if there’s a slowdown factor, it would be the AGI’s own value system. Even if I could rewrite my own brain arbitrarily fast, I probably wouldn’t. I want to survive. I care about my mental well-being and that of my family and friends. There’s an argument for safety and common sense: you make small changes and improvements, see how they pan out in the real world, make other small changes, see how they pan out, and roll back if they aren’t working out. The transition from AGI to ASI will probably be gated by responsible self-modification on the part of the AGI. This is where we hit the big challenge that I see will happen in this transition period. I think you have the following sort of Scylla versus Charybdis issue, a rock-and-a-hard-place issue. If you have multiple competing efforts at AGI, for example, an AGI arms race between the US and China such as certain national leaders are currently advocating, and multiple parties get a human-level AGI around the same time, which is almost guaranteed to happen, then you’d need agreement from all the parties controlling the AGIs about moderating the pace of development to have a moderated pace of advanced superintelligence. Even if you kept everything locked down, that doesn’t work too well. Someone gets poached by someone else and offered $10 million to share the trade secrets. We can see with transformers from Google to OpenAI, then back to Google and to DeepSeek and so on. You can keep things locked down a little while, but not that long. If you have multiple competing parties building AGIs, there’s a really annoying arms-race psychology. From where I stand right now, it might look different once we have the AGI, but it seems to me the most likely, most responsible thing to do is not go from AGI to superintelligence at the maximum possible speed. Probably the most responsible thing to do will be to do that by baby steps and use some experimental information gathering as you go. Maybe the AGI will just print out a very compelling argument why upgrading to superintelligence in one fell swoop is the best thing. Maybe it’ll be right. But supposing that some gradual increase from AGI to ASI is the best thing to do, that requires a lot of trust among the competing parties. The US’s AGI isn’t going to want to go slowly if it thinks China’s AGI is going fast. And a decentralized network building AGI isn’t going to vote to go slowly if it thinks the centralized network that wants to make it illegal and put its developers in jail is going fast. This is potentially dangerous and annoying, because we already have the makings of an AGI arms race. Before we actually have AGI, it’s mostly a matter of humans using tools to advance their own particular sectarian interests. But if that’s transmitted into the AGIs where they’re driving their own development, what exactly happens? Each AGI, to the extent it implicitly or explicitly wants to keep surviving, will see that the other AGI getting to the singularity first is a threat to its own survival and to the survival of the people it loves who created it. The AGI might think, “Just to save the life of my creators, who I’ve been trained to empathize with, I need to make myself smarter and smarter before this other AGI that’s ruled by these guys who literally want to kill my creators.” This is sort of what our geopolitical system is tending toward now. There’s a possibility that having the first AGI be a sort of decentralized, open global brain can diffuse that dynamic, because you’ll have a decentralized, open thing which is just smarter than any of the sectarian AIs, and then more resources get pitched into the open decentralized global brain and the sectarian ones can’t catch up. That’s a possibility, but there are a lot of different uncertainties there that anyone could think of immediately.

items.question: Why do you doubt that Steve Omohundro and Max Tegmark’s proposal for provably secure technological infrastructure is viable in the near term?
items.object: Provably secure infrastructure for the world's technology
items.answer: I love the idea. I’ve done research myself on how to make systems provably secure, both in quantum computing and in LLMs and so forth. I don’t think that’s terribly viable to roll out in the near term. I argued this with Steve, who I’ve known a long time, in an interview we did, for a couple reasons. One is it’s just a lot more expensive to do things in a secure way. I posted a paper recently on secure transformer architecture that will only slow things down by a factor of two or so, just to make a transformer that isn’t so susceptible to prompt-injection attacks. That’s just slowing down by a factor of two to protect against one kind of attack vector. It’s not provably secure. If you look at homomorphic encryption, which you need to make AI processes really secure with respect to other people hacking in and spying and seeing what they’re doing, right now that slows you down by a factor of several hundred. I did some interesting calculations suggesting you could do homomorphic encryption of complex programs with only maybe one order of magnitude slowdown on a quantum computer. Interestingly, it might be that some of this security is easier when you’re into quantum computing just because of the different way quantum computers operate. Even so, it’s just way more expensive to do things in a provably secure way. Add on top of it that we don’t really know how to do it yet for most of the processes in our global tech stack. It’s a really interesting research area, but it is a research area. You’d be asking the world to pause all sorts of development and instead put huge amounts of money into research on fundamental provability of safety of different parts of our tech stack, at a time when the US is cutting funding for the NSF for all sorts of basic research. Doesn’t seem plausible in that sense. And there’s also the arms-race dynamic. If the US chose to slow itself down by making everything provably secure, and China or Russia didn’t, the US is quickly going to decide that’s stupid.

items.question: What do you see as the most plausible way for the first AGI to enable a beneficial transition to superintelligence?
items.object: The first AGI as a steward of a beneficial transition to superintelligence
items.answer: Seems like the most plausible course to a beneficial outcome I can see is the first AGI is created by some group that wants to make it open and decentralized and doesn’t care about controlling it personally, and doesn’t care about putting their own personal value systems in it as opposed to all the other human values. Then this first AGI has got to rapidly make a plan for secure, beneficial AGI development and rollout across the world, and then people have to choose to adopt that. I don’t think that’s unthinkable. Suppose your first AGI thinks provable security is important, and that first AGI then solves these tech problems faster than humans have been able to and tells you how to make chips and operating systems and LLMs and reasoning systems that are provably secure in infrastructure. “Here’s provably secure embedded Linux version one.” If the first AGI is oriented towards benefit and safety for humans as well as AGIs, figures out how to make the right sort of infrastructure, and manages to roll that out, then you could have a more beneficial transition. If you want to go science-fictional, this can be achieved in various ways. You could say the first AGI release is a botnet that just replaces everyone’s OS with a provably secure OS, and then bada bing, you’re done. That’s how it would work in a science-fiction story, and it could happen. You can’t rule it out. There’s also a possible future where this comes out like global nuclear disarmament or treaties on biological weaponry. Once you really have the AGI and it’s there in front of you, it’s really clear, “Whoa, this thing is smarter than people.” Then suddenly the people running major world governments are like, “Well, okay, yes, we will adopt this safety protocol,” and the AGI presumably would roll out technology that allowed monitoring of whether the safety protocol was actually being adopted. That’s at least a plausible avenue: the first AGI leads a process of enforcing some reasonable safety for the next stage. The reason I think that’s more plausible after the first AGI is launched is that I’m hoping the first AGI can just make security by design not be obscenely expensive and difficult, which it is right now. For humans to make it not obscenely expensive and difficult will take a long time, and the AI industry isn’t going to pause for it.
